newsitem.title: UK: Northern Ireland's Hume confident of new IRA ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Northern Ireland's Hume confident of new IRA ceasefire.

text.p: A Catholic political leader said on Thursday he believed that the Irish Republican Army (IRA) was ready to call a new ceasefire if the British government accepted proposals he had made.

John Hume, leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party, said he had proposed that Britain set a rigid timetable for the all-party peace talks on the future of Northern Ireland, according to media reports.
In exchange, he said the IRA would renew the truce it abandoned in February so that its political arm, Sinn Fein, could join the talks.
"I will put my head on the line for this. I am absolutely convinced now we can achieve an absolutely genuine, unequivocal restoration (of the ceasefire)," he told the BBC.
Hume has been holding talks with Sinn Fein chief Gerry Adams and British and Irish leaders to try to breathe some life into the faltering peace process.
He was talking just a few hours after bomb disposal experts defused a 600-lb (250-kg) car bomb planted outside police headquarters in a heavily populated part of the city of Londonderry.
The Irish Continuity Army Council (CAC), a splinter republican group, said it planted the bomb.
Hume called the group "enemies of all the people of Ireland" and appealed to pro-British Protestant guerrillas not to retaliate.
The Protestant "Loyalists" have honoured a two-year ceasefire which has enabled their political allies to take part in the peace talks.
"I certainly hope that they will maintain their ceasefire..," Hume said.

Security analysts said the emergence of the hawkish CAC, whose supporters are said to have broken away from the IRA 10 years ago to protest a "peace strategy" advocated by Sinn Fein, represented a dangerous twist to the delicate search for peace.
Protestant leaders said they could not predict whether pro-British guerrillas would retaliate to the Londonderry bomb.

"They have resisted this type of goading before and we all must hope and pray that they will continue to so," said David Adams, a leader of the Ulster Democratic Party, the political wing of the outlawed Protestant Ulster Defence Association.
Sinn Fein said the incident underlined the urgent need for a negotiated Northern Ireland settlement.

"It shows the need for all those interested in peace to redouble their efforts to remove all preconditions and obstacles to a truly meaningful peace process," said Gerry O'Hara, chairman of Sinn Fein in Northern Ireland.
